# Preface {.unnumbered}

Sample-size planning is a recurring challenge in postgraduate medical education. Investigators are often presented with a formula before they have clearly identified the question that formula should answer. The more important decisions concern the outcome, estimand, sampling design, credible prior information and acceptable uncertainty.

This manual is intended to support foundation-course teaching and practical protocol development. Most chapters can be read in one sitting. Clinical scenarios introduce each method, mathematical expressions are explained in context, and self-check exercises invite the reader to justify the calculation rather than copy a result.

The book is companion material to an open-source R/Shiny application, but does not presume that software selection guarantees correct methods. Each calculation is conditional on its assumptions. Non-inferiority margins, cluster sampling, diagnostic disease strata and choices of confidence-interval method receive particular attention because they are common sources of misinterpretation.

## Editorial status

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This edition is a **scientific and structural baseline**. The 300-slide resident/foundation-course teaching archive and its original worked examples have **not yet been imported**. Numerical examples that are already included are labelled illustrative. The full review record is maintained in `editorial/chapter-status.csv`, and the practical submission checklist in `editorial/REVIEW-PROTOCOL.md`.
:::

## Conventions

- $n_0$: unadjusted planning size (usually unrounded).
- $n_{complete}$: required usable observations after final whole-number rounding.
- $n_{recruit}$: planned number to recruit after separately justified losses.
- $\alpha$: selected type I error rate; $1-\beta$: power under the chosen alternative.
- Group differences are always defined by group order and outcome direction.
- Probability inputs are stated on the 0–1 scale in mathematical expressions; calculator interface units must be checked separately.

References are consolidated at the end of the book. All calculations and claims remain subject to editorial and independent statistical review.
